Building OCCDS (Occurrence Data) ADaMs in R: Handling Adverse Events the R Way
Building OCCDS (Occurrence Data) ADaMs in R: Handling Adverse Events the R Way
text:
Building ADAE with {admiral}
The {admiral} package streamlines OCCDS derivations. The workflow generally follows: 1. Load AE and ADSL. 2. Merge ADSL variables (like TRTSDT) into AE. 3. Derive partial dates/times (ASTDT, AENDT). 4. Derive population and occurrence flags (TRTEMFL, CQ01NAM).
Here is a simplified R script:

library(dplyr)
library(admiral)
library(lubridate)

# Mock Data
ae <- data.frame(
  USUBJID = c("101", "101", "102"),
  AETERM = c("HEADACHE", "NAUSEA", "FATIGUE"),
  AESTDTC = c("2024-01-10", "2024-01-20", "2024-02-05")
)

adsl <- data.frame(
  USUBJID = c("101", "102"),
  TRTSDT = as.Date(c("2024-01-15", "2024-02-01"))
)

# 1. Merge ADSL
adae <- ae %>%
  derive_vars_merged(
    dataset_add = adsl,
    by_vars = exprs(USUBJID),
    new_vars = exprs(TRTSDT)
  ) %>%
  
  # 2. Convert ISO character dates to numeric R dates
  mutate(ASTDT = as.Date(AESTDTC)) %>%
  
  # 3. Derive Treatment Emergent Flag (TRTEMFL)
  derive_var_extreme_flag(
    by_vars = exprs(USUBJID),
    order = exprs(ASTDT),
    new_var = TRTEMFL,
    condition = ASTDT >= TRTSDT,
    mode = "first" # Just an example if we wanted the first event
  )

print(adae)

Wait, derive_var_extreme_flag() isn’t quite right for a TEAE flag since TEAEs apply to all events that occur after treatment, not just the “extreme” first or last one.
Instead, {admiral} provides elegant logical evaluation via standard {dplyr} mutate(). Because {admiral} handles the complex merging (like the derive_vars_merged step above), the actual flag derivation is dead simple.

adae <- adae %>%
  mutate(
    TRTEMFL = if_else(ASTDT >= TRTSDT & !is.na(ASTDT), "Y", "N", missing = "N")
  )

title: Building OCCDS (Occurrence Data) ADaMs in R: Handling Adverse Events the R Way
text:
Handling First Occurrence Flags
Where {admiral} really shines is with extreme flags. In typical TFLs, we often report “Subjects with at least one AE.” To do this, we need a flag (AOCCIFL) that indicates the first occurrence of any AE for a subject.
In SAS, this requires PROC SORT followed by first.USUBJID.
In {admiral}:

adae_first <- adae %>%
  filter(TRTEMFL == "Y") %>%
  derive_var_extreme_flag(
    by_vars = exprs(USUBJID),
    order = exprs(ASTDT),
    new_var = AOCCIFL,
    mode = "first"
  )

adae <- adae %>%
  left_join(adae_first, by = names(adae)) %>%
  mutate(AOCCIFL = if_else(is.na(AOCCIFL), "", AOCCIFL))

print(adae)

This single function handles the sorting, grouping by USUBJID, checking the condition (TRTEMFL == "Y"), and flagging only the first record chronologically (mode = "first").

title: Building OCCDS (Occurrence Data) ADaMs in R: Handling Adverse Events the R Way
text:
Summarizing AE Counts
Once ADAE is built, we frequently need to count the number of AEs per subject and push that count back into ADSL.

# Add total AEs per subject back to ADSL
adsl_updated <- adsl %>%
  derive_var_merged_summary(
    dataset_add = adae,
    by_vars = exprs(USUBJID),
    new_var = AETOT,
    analysis_var = USUBJID,
    summary_fun = function(x) length(x)
  ) %>%
  mutate(AETOT = if_else(is.na(AETOT), 0, AETOT))

print(adsl_updated)

The derive_var_merged_summary() function eliminates the need for separate PROC SQL count(*) block and subsequent merge.
OCCDS derivations in R highlight a massive shift from multi-step data processing (sort -> merge -> derive) to a single, continuous, highly readable text pipeline.
Next, we dive into the most complex of all ADaM structures: Basic Data Structure (BDS).

title: Mapping Raw Data to SDTM in R: A SAS Programmer’s Guide
text:
For over two decades, SAS has been the unchallenged king of mapping raw clinical data (often from EDC systems like Medidata Rave or Veeva Vault) into the Study Data Tabulation Model (SDTM) format required by regulatory agencies like the FDA.
Creating SDTM datasets involves joining multiple raw forms, deriving standard variables like STUDYID, DOMAIN, and USUBJID, applying dictionaries (MedDRA, WHODrug), and carefully structuring columns according to the CDISC Implementation Guide (IG).
So… how do we do this without SAS?

title: Mapping Raw Data to SDTM in R: A SAS Programmer’s Guide
section: The Mental Map: SAS Data Steps vs R

title: Mapping Raw Data to SDTM in R: A SAS Programmer’s Guide
text:
The R Implementation
Here is how we build the conceptual equivalent in R.

library(dplyr)
library(lubridate)
library(stringr)

# Simulating raw data
raw_demog <- data.frame(
  subject = c("001", "002", "003"),
  sex_raw = c("M", "F", "F"),
  BRTHDAT = as.Date(c("1980-01-15", "1975-06-20", "1990-11-05")),
  RANDDAT = as.Date(c("2024-01-10", "2024-01-12", "2024-01-15"))
)

# Creating the DM Domain
dm_domain <- raw_demog %>%
  # Rename columns (new_name = old_name)
  rename(
    SUBJID = subject,
    SEX = sex_raw
  ) %>%
  # Derive new columns
  mutate(
    STUDYID = "ABC-123",
    DOMAIN = "DM",
    USUBJID = paste(STUDYID, SUBJID, sep = "-"),
    
    # Date formatting to ISO 8601 (often YYYY-MM-DD)
    BRTHDTC = as.character(BRTHDAT),
    RFSTDTC = as.character(RANDDAT),
    
    # Age derivation using lubridate
    AGE = time_length(interval(BRTHDAT, RANDDAT), "years") %>% floor()
  ) %>%
  # Select and order final columns
  select(STUDYID, DOMAIN, USUBJID, SUBJID, RFSTDTC, BRTHDTC, AGE, SEX)

print(dm_domain)

  STUDYID DOMAIN     USUBJID SUBJID    RFSTDTC    BRTHDTC AGE SEX
1 ABC-123     DM ABC-123-001    001 2024-01-10 1980-01-15  43   M
2 ABC-123     DM ABC-123-002    002 2024-01-12 1975-06-20  48   F
3 ABC-123     DM ABC-123-003    003 2024-01-15 1990-11-05  33   F



Key Differences and Advantages

paste() replaces catx(): In R, paste() or paste0() (or stringr::str_c()) is used to concatenate strings to build the USUBJID.
lubridate makes dates easier: Calculating age in SAS requires remembering esoteric functions like yrdif. In R, {lubridate} makes time intervals mathematically logical.
No Length / Type Declarations: In SAS, you must declare length DOMAIN $2. to avoid truncation. R dynamically handles string lengths, so you never have to worry about a string being truncated because of an earlier column definition.
Column Selection: The select() function perfectly replaces the keep and retain statements, simultaneously defining which columns to keep and what order they should appear in.

title: Mapping Raw Data to SDTM in R: A SAS Programmer’s Guide
text:
Handing ISO 8601 Dates
One of the most complex parts of SDTM is formatting partial dates into ISO 8601 character strings (e.g., 2024-05 if the day is missing). In SAS, this usually involves painful substring manipulation.
In R, packages like {parsedate} or custom {stringr} functions make this incredibly concise.

# Simple example of handling a missing day
raw_dates <- c("2024-Jan-01", "2024-Feb-Unknown")

# Using stringr to extract Year and Month 
clean_dates <- raw_dates %>%
  str_replace_all("-Unknown", "") %>%
  as.Date(format = "%Y-%b-%d") # The second one will become NA

print(clean_dates)

[1] "2024-01-01" NA          


(Note: Clinical date imputation can get complex depending on your SAP, but vectorized string manipulation in R is infinitely more powerful than SAS’s substr and index functions).

title: Mapping Raw Data to SDTM in R: A SAS Programmer’s Guide
text:
Conclusion
Migrating SDTM generation to R forces you to write code in functional pipelines. The code becomes highly readable, self-documenting, and free from the strict column-length restrictions of SAS data types.

title: Creating ADSL (Subject Level Analysis Dataset) in R: Moving Away from SAS
text:
What is {admiral}?
The {admiral} package is part of the Pharmaverse—a collaborative effort by major pharmaceutical companies to create a standardized suite of R packages for clinical reporting. {admiral} provides modular, pre-tested functions specifically designed to build ADaM datasets following CDISC standards.
Let’s look at how to build ADSL.

title: Creating ADSL (Subject Level Analysis Dataset) in R: Moving Away from SAS
text:
Step 1: Merging the Raw SDTMs
In SAS, you might merge your datasets. In R, we use joins.

library(dplyr)
library(admiral)

Warning: package 'admiral' was built under R version 4.4.3

library(lubridate)

# Simulating SDTM Data
dm <- data.frame(
  USUBJID = c("001", "002"),
  ARM = c("Placebo", "Active"),
  AGE = c(45, 60),
  SEX = c("M", "F")
)

ds <- data.frame(
  USUBJID = c("001", "001", "002", "002"),
  DSCAT = c("DISPOSITION EVENT", "OTHER EVENT", "DISPOSITION EVENT", "OTHER EVENT"),
  DSDECOD = c("COMPLETED", "RANDOMIZED", "ADVERSE EVENT", "RANDOMIZED")
)

title: Creating ADSL (Subject Level Analysis Dataset) in R: Moving Away from SAS
text:
Step 2: Deriving Flags using {admiral}
Instead of writing custom conditional logic to figure out if someone completed the study, {admiral} gives us functions like derive_var_merged_cat().
Let’s derive COMPLFL (Completer Flag) based on the Disposition (DS) domain.

# Build ADSL using a dplyr pipeline
adsl <- dm %>%
  # 1. Convert ARM to TRT01P (Planned Treatment)
  mutate(TRT01P = ARM) %>%
  
  # 2. Derive Completer Flag (COMPLFL) from DS
  derive_var_merged_exist_flag(
    dataset_add = ds,
    by_vars = exprs(USUBJID),
    new_var = COMPLFL,
    condition = DSCAT == "DISPOSITION EVENT" & DSDECOD == "COMPLETED"
  )

print(adsl)

  USUBJID     ARM AGE SEX  TRT01P COMPLFL
1     001 Placebo  45   M Placebo       Y
2     002  Active  60   F  Active    <NA>


Notice how derive_var_merged_exist_flag() handles the logic seamlessly. We tell it: - Which dataset to look at (dataset_add = ds) - How to link them (by_vars = exprs(USUBJID)) - What to name the new flag (new_var = COMPLFL) - What condition triggers a “Y” (condition = ...)
If the condition is met, the subject gets a Y. If not, they get an NA (which you can easily convert to an N if your SAP requires it).

title: Creating ADSL (Subject Level Analysis Dataset) in R: Moving Away from SAS
text:
Step 3: Deriving Age Categories
SAS requires PROC FORMAT or nested if/else loops to create AGEGR1 (e.g., <65, >=65).
In R, it’s a breeze.

adsl <- adsl %>%
  mutate(
    AGEGR1 = case_when(
      AGE < 65 ~ "<65",
      AGE >= 65 ~ ">=65",
      TRUE ~ "Missing"
    )
  )

print(adsl)

  USUBJID     ARM AGE SEX  TRT01P COMPLFL AGEGR1
1     001 Placebo  45   M Placebo       Y    <65
2     002  Active  60   F  Active    <NA>    <65

title: Creating ADSL (Subject Level Analysis Dataset) in R: Moving Away from SAS
text:
Why {admiral} Beats Custom Macros
In SAS programming, companies build massive libraries of proprietary macros (like %derive_trt() or %derive_flags()). These macros are notoriously difficult to debug, poorly documented, and non-transferable between companies.
By using {admiral} in R: 1. It’s open source: The code is transparent and peer-reviewed by the industry. 2. Standardized: A programmer from Company A can read Company B’s ADSL code because they both use {admiral} syntax. 3. Traceable: Every {admiral} function integrates beautifully with {dplyr} pipes, making the transformation logic incredibly easy to read from top to bottom.
ADSL is only the beginning. In the next post, we’ll tackle OCCDS (Occurrence Data) domains like ADAE!

title: TFL Generation with R: A SAS Programmer’s Overview
TFL Generation with R: A SAS Programmer’s Overview
TFL Generation with R: A SAS Programmer’s Overview
text:
The R TFL Ecosystem
R approaches TFL generation totally differently. Instead of relying on a single, massive procedure like PROC REPORT, R provides specialized packages tailored for specific types of outputs.

1. Tables: {rtables} vs {gt} vs {gtsummary}
Tables are incredibly complex structural objects in clinical trials. They are not just data frames; they have spanning headers (“Active vs Placebo”), footnotes, multiple nested rows (System Organ Class > Preferred Term), and specific alignment rules.

{rtables}: Built by the Pharmaverse community (heavily supported by Roche). It is explicitly designed to replicate the complex, nested trees of clinical trial tables. It is declarative (you define the layout first, then apply the data).
{gt} (Grammar of Tables): Built by Posit. It is excellent for highly customized, beautiful static tables. It treats tables like ggplot treats charts—building them piece by piece (title, spanners, body, stub, footnotes).
{gtsummary}: A wrapper package that takes an ADaM dataset and automatically calculates standard summary statistics (mean, SD, n, p-values) and outputs a {gt} or {flextable} object. Perfect for quick Demographic tables.



2. Figures: {ggplot2}
When it comes to Figures, SAS isn’t even in the same league as R. PROC SGPLOT is highly functional, but R’s {ggplot2} (Grammar of Graphics) is arguably the most powerful data visualization framework on the planet.
With {ggplot2}, creating Kaplan-Meier curves, Waterfall plots, and adverse event volcano plots isn’t just possible—it’s intuitive. We will explore {survival} and {survminer} for efficacy plots later in this series.


3. Listings: {flextable} and Quarto
Listings are essentially the raw data dumped into a PDF or Word document with pagination.
In SAS, this is PROC PRINT or PROC REPORT. In R, you can use packages like {flextable} which export perfectly to Microsoft Word (Docx) with repeating column headers on new pages.
However, the biggest paradigm shift in R is Quarto (the successor to R Markdown). Quarto allows you to generate paginated RTF, PDF, or Word documents dynamically. Instead of creating 50 separate RTF files using ODS, you can knit a single Quarto document that loops through your datasets and generates 50 listings with automatic tables of contents.

title: TFL Generation with R: A SAS Programmer’s Overview
text:
The Workflow Shift
In SAS: 1. Load dataset. 2. Run PROC SUMMARY to get stats. 3. Run Data step to format stats into strings ("15 (30.0%)"). 4. Run PROC TRANSPOSE to put Placebo and Active side-by-side. 5. Run PROC SORT to order the rows correctly. 6. Run PROC REPORT with an ODS RTF wrapper to print.
In R (e.g., using {rtables}): 1. Load dataset. 2. Define the tree layout (lyt <- basic_table() %>% split_cols_by("ARM") %>% analyze("AGE")). 3. Build the table (build_table(lyt, adsl)). 4. Export to RTF or PDF.
In R, the computation (summary stats) and the rendering (printing the table) happen in a single step.
Next, we’ll look at real code for building an Adverse Event Summary table using {rtables}!

title: Efficacy TFLs: Creating Waterfall and Spider Plots for Tumor Response
text:
Survival curves tell us when a patient failed therapy. But in early-phase solid tumor oncology trials (measuring RECIST criteria), we are deeply interested in how much their tumors grew or shrank over time relative to baseline.
Two plots dominated this space: The Waterfall Plot (Best Overall Response per patient) and the Spider Plot (Tumor burden trajectory over time).
Getting these right in SAS PROC SGPLOT requires massive data manipulation to generate sorted dummy variables for the categorical axes. In {ggplot2}, it’s incredibly straightforward.

text:
Survival curves tell us when a patient failed therapy. But in early-phase solid tumor oncology trials (measuring RECIST criteria), we are deeply interested in how much their tumors grew or shrank over time relative to baseline.
Two plots dominated this space: The Waterfall Plot (Best Overall Response per patient) and the Spider Plot (Tumor burden trajectory over time).
Getting these right in SAS PROC SGPLOT requires massive data manipulation to generate sorted dummy variables for the categorical axes. In {ggplot2}, it’s incredibly straightforward.

title: Efficacy TFLs: Creating Waterfall and Spider Plots for Tumor Response
text:
The Waterfall Plot
A Waterfall Plot aligns every patient on the X-axis (sorted by their tumor shrinkage) and plots a vertical bar representing their maximum percentage change from baseline in the sum of target lesion diameters.

library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(forcats)

# Simulated ADTR (Tumor Response) data
set.seed(42)
adtr_bor <- data.frame(
  USUBJID = paste0("S-", 1:40),
  PCHG = rnorm(40, mean = -10, sd = 30), # % Change from Baseline
  BOR = sample(c("CR", "PR", "SD", "PD"), 40, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.1, 0.3, 0.4, 0.2))
)

# Cap growth at +100% just for visualization scaling (Standard practice)
adtr_bor <- adtr_bor %>%
  mutate(PCHG_CAP = if_else(PCHG > 100, 100, PCHG))

# The key step for Waterfall: Reordering the X-axis by the Y-value
# We use forcats::fct_reorder to sort USUBJID factor levels by PCHG_CAP (descending)
ggplot(adtr_bor, aes(x = fct_reorder(USUBJID, -PCHG_CAP), y = PCHG_CAP, fill = BOR)) +
  
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", width = 0.8) +
  
  # Standard RECIST reference lines 
  # PR boundary: -30%
  # PD boundary: +20%
  geom_hline(yintercept = -30, linetype = "dashed", color = "black") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 20, linetype = "dashed", color = "black") +
  
  # Axis modifications
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(-100, 100, 20), limits = c(-100, 100)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("CR" = "#1A85FF", "PR" = "#D41159", "SD" = "#FFC20A", "PD" = "#000000")) +
  
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_blank(), # Hide individual subject IDs
    axis.ticks.x = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank()
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Best Overall Response (Waterfall Plot)",
    x = "Individual Subjects",
    y = "Maximum % Change in Sum of Lesions from Baseline",
    fill = "Best Response"
  )








The trick here is fct_reorder(). In SAS, sorting a categorical axis by a numeric value requires creating an artificial order variable, sorting the dataset, and enforcing X-axis tick ordering. R handles it as an aesthetic mapping.

title: Efficacy TFLs: Creating Waterfall and Spider Plots for Tumor Response
text:
The Spider Plot
A Spider Plot draws a line for each individual subject, tracking their tumor percent change across study visits.

# Simulated longitudinal ADTR data
adtr_long <- data.frame(
  USUBJID = rep(paste0("S-", 1:10), each = 5),
  AVISITN = rep(seq(0, 24, by = 6), 10),
  PCHG = runif(50, -60, 40)
) %>%
  # Force baseline to 0
  mutate(PCHG = if_else(AVISITN == 0, 0, PCHG))

# Sorting subjects into "Responders" vs "Non-Responders" just for color coding
adtr_long <- adtr_long %>%
  group_by(USUBJID) %>%
  mutate(MIN_PCHG = min(PCHG)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(RespGroup = if_else(MIN_PCHG <= -30, "Objective Response", "No Objective Response"))


ggplot(adtr_long, aes(x = AVISITN, y = PCHG, group = USUBJID, color = RespGroup)) +
  geom_line(size = 0.8, alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.9) +
  
  # Standard RECIST reference lines
  geom_hline(yintercept = -30, linetype = "dashed", color = "black") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 20, linetype = "dashed", color = "black") +
  
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Objective Response" = "#1A85FF", "No Objective Response" = "#D41159")) +
  
  theme_bw() +
  labs(
    title = "Longitudinal Tumor Burden (Spider Plot)",
    x = "Study Visit (Weeks)",
    y = "% Change in Sum of Lesions from Baseline",
    color = "Response Status"
  )

Warning: Using `size` aesthetic for lines was deprecated in ggplot2 3.4.0.
ℹ Please use `linewidth` instead.









With ggplot2, the group = USUBJID mapping instinctively knows to draw a unique, connected line for each subject across the discrete time points (AVISITN), ensuring zero “jump” lines between data points.
With both SAS and R now capable of creating these visualizations, the critical difference is sheer speed of development. Once your ggplot2 syntax is locked in, R produces these complex oncology metrics significantly faster and with less code complexity than traditional SAS macros.

section: Welcome to R: The Infection of NA
text:
Welcome to R: The Infection of NA
In R, missing data is denoted by NA (Not Available). And unlike SAS, R operates under the philosophy that missing data is infectious. If you don’t know part of an equation, you logically cannot know the result.

# R Code
x <- 10
y <- NA

# Basic arithmetic
total <- sum(x, y) 
mean_val <- mean(c(x, y))

print(total)

[1] NA

# [1] NA
print(mean_val)

[1] NA

# [1] NA

R refuses to guess. If you ask it for the sum of 10 and an unknown number, it sensibly concludes the answer is unknown.

The Fix: na.rm = TRUE
To make R behave somewhat like SAS, you simply have to instruct it to “remove NAs” before performing an operation. This is done with the na.rm = TRUE argument inside functions like sum(), mean(), and sd().

# R Code
total_rm      <- sum(x, y, na.rm = TRUE)
mean_val_rm   <- mean(c(x, y), na.rm = TRUE)

print(total_rm)

[1] 10

# [1] 10
print(mean_val_rm)

[1] 10

# [1] 10

This is incredibly important when summarizing clinical data. If one patient out of 500 is missing a baseline lab value, your overall baseline mean calculation will fail (NA) unless you explicitly set na.rm = TRUE.

title: Handling Missing Data: How R Does It Differently Than SAS
text:
The Great Equality Trap
Here is another massive gotcha for SAS programmers.
In SAS, if you want to find all rows where AGE is missing, you do this:
/* SAS Code */
data missing_age;
  set adsl;
  if age = .;
run;
If you try to perfectly translate that to R, you will crash and burn.

# Bad R Code - Do not do this
# adsl %>% filter(age == NA)

Why doesn’t this work? In R, the expression NA == NA evaluates to NA. You cannot check if something is equal to “unknown.” So comparing age == NA doesn’t return TRUE or FALSE; it returns a vector of NAs, which causes filter() to fail.
To check for missingness in R, you must use the is.na() function.

# Mock ADSL Data
library(dplyr)

adsl <- data.frame(
  usubjid = 1:5,
  age = c(45, NA, 60, NA, 30),
  status = c("Completed", "Dropout", "Completed", "Randomized", "Dropout"),
  weight = c(80, 75, 90, 85, 78)
)

# Correct R Code
# To find missing values
# missing_age <- adsl %>% filter(is.na(age))

# To drop missing values
# complete_age <- adsl %>% filter(!is.na(age))
# or using tidyr
# complete_age <- adsl %>% drop_na(age)

title: Handling Missing Data: How R Does It Differently Than SAS
text:
Creating Missing Data
In SAS, you might conditionally wipe out a value like this:
/* SAS Code */
if (status = 'Dropout') then weight = .;
In R, we typically use {dplyr}’s mutate() and ifelse() or if_else() or case_when().

# R Code
# adsl <- adsl %>%
#  mutate(weight = if_else(status == "Dropout", NA_real_, weight))

Wait, what is NA_real_?
R is a strictly typed language. Under the hood, standard NA is a logical vector. When you are replacing numeric values (reals), {dplyr} functions like if_else() (which are stricter than base R’s ifelse()) require the replacement value to be of the exact same type as the original column. Thus, you use NA_real_ for double precision floating-point numbers, NA_integer_ for whole numbers, and NA_character_ for text.

title: Handling Missing Data: How R Does It Differently Than SAS
text:
Final Thoughts
R’s strict handling of missing data forces you to be deliberate. In clinical reporting, this is a massive advantage! You want to be violently thrown an error if you try to average a column containing hidden missing data, because quietly dropping it could lead to incorrect efficacy results.
In the next post, we’ll cover how to replicate SAS’s mighty PROC FORMAT.

text:
We spend hours making Laboratory Shift Tables—those massive matrices showing how many subjects went from “Low” at baseline to “High” at Week 12.
The problem? Most medical reviewers glance at these 100-page tables and immediately look for a figure instead. Large cross-tabulations are terrible at conveying magnitude. Yes, 5 patients shifted to “High” ALT, but did they barely cross the threshold, or did their liver enzymes spike 10x the Upper Limit of Normal (ULN)?
In SAS, creating complex interactive or highly customized graphics (PROC SGPLOT / GTL) is cumbersome. In R, we have the gold standard: {ggplot2}.

section: Building a Spaghetti Plot for Vitals
text:
Building a Spaghetti Plot for Vitals
Let’s map out how a SAS programmer would build a trend plot of Systolic Blood Pressure (SBP) over time for individual patients, overlaid with a mean trend line.

library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

# Simulated Vitals Data
set.seed(123)
advs <- data.frame(
  USUBJID = rep(c("101", "102", "103", "104", "105"), each = 4),
  TRTA = rep(c("Placebo", "Active", "Placebo", "Active", "Active"), each = 4),
  AVISITN = rep(c(0, 4, 8, 12), times = 5),
  AVISIT = rep(c("Baseline", "Week 4", "Week 8", "Week 12"), times = 5)
) %>%
  mutate(AVAL = round(rnorm(n(), mean = 120, sd = 15))) # Random SBP values

# Ensure AVISIT is ordered correctly as a factor!
advs$AVISIT <- factor(advs$AVISIT, levels = c("Baseline", "Week 4", "Week 8", "Week 12"))


The {ggplot2} Pipeline
In {ggplot2}, we define the dataset, map the axes (aesthetics or aes()), and then add geometric layers (geom_line(), geom_point()).

# Basic Spaghetti Plot
ggplot(advs, aes(x = AVISIT, y = AVAL, group = USUBJID, color = TRTA)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.5) +  # Faded lines for individual subjects
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) + # Faded points
  
  # Overlay a LOESS smoothing curve (overall trend) grouping by TRTA
  geom_smooth(aes(group = TRTA), method = "loess", se = FALSE, size = 1.5) +
  
  # Clinical Formatting
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Systolic Blood Pressure Trends by Treatment Arm",

section: Visualizing Lab Shifts: The Boxplot Approach
text:
Visualizing Lab Shifts: The Boxplot Approach
Shift tables lack magnitude. A better approach is to plot the actual lab values at Baseline vs. Maximum Post-Baseline grouped by their Baseline Status.
Let’s say we have derived baseline grades for Bilirubin (BILI). We want to see the distribution of maximum post-baseline values.

# Simulated Lab Data
adlb_max <- data.frame(
  USUBJID = 1:50,
  TRTA = sample(c("Placebo", "Active"), 50, replace = TRUE),
  BBASE_GRADE = sample(c("Normal", "High"), 50, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.8, 0.2)),
  AVAL = rnorm(50, mean = 1.5, sd = 0.5) # Max Post-Baseline values
)

ggplot(adlb_max, aes(x = BBASE_GRADE, y = AVAL, fill = TRTA)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.color = "red", outlier.size = 2) +
  
  # Add a horizontal line representing the Upper Limit of Normal (e.g., 1.2)
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1.2, linetype = "dashed", color = "black") +
  
  annotate("text", x = 1, y = 1.25, label = "ULN Threshold", size = 3, hjust = 0) +
  
  theme_bw() +
  labs(
    title = "Max Post-Baseline Bilirubin by Baseline Grade",
    subtitle = "Red points indicate significant outliers",
    x = "Baseline Grade",
    y = "Maximum Post-Baseline Bilirubin (mg/dL)",
    fill = "Treatment Arm"
  )









Why this beats a table
If a reviewer looks at this plot, they can instantly see: 1. Did the “Normal” baseline subjects trend higher in the Active arm? (Look at the median line of the boxplot). 2. Are there any catastrophic outliers? (The red dots). 3. How many people crossed the ULN threshold who were previously normal? (The distribution above the dashed line).

title: Replicating SAS Formats and Informats in R (Using Factors and Lookups)
text:
There are few features SAS programmers love more than PROC FORMAT. It allows you to store the underlying raw data (like 1, 2, 3) but display beautiful, human-readable labels ("Mild", "Moderate", "Severe") in all your outputs, without modifying the actual dataset. It’s clean, efficient, and essential for clinical TFLs.
When attempting to do this in R, SAS programmers often try to permanently overwrite the column string with nested conditional logic. “Wait, do I actually have to replace my 1s with ‘Mild’ in the dataframe?”
The answer is: Not necessarily! R has robust systems for handling categorical data and lookups that mimic what PROC FORMAT does, but they work quite differently.

title: Replicating SAS Formats and Informats in R (Using Factors and Lookups)
text:
Method 1: Factors (The Closest Native Equivalent)
In R, a factor is used to store categorical data. It is literally an integer vector with an associated set of character “labels” (or levels). This makes it conceptually very similar to applying a format.
/* SAS Code */
proc format;
  value sev
    1 = "Mild"
    2 = "Moderate"
    3 = "Severe";
run;

data adae;
  set adae;
  format aesev sev.;
run;
In R, we create factors either using base R factor() or the {forcats} package (part of the tidyverse).

# R Code
library(dplyr)


Attaching package: 'dplyr'


The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':

    filter, lag


The following objects are masked from 'package:base':

    intersect, setdiff, setequal, union

library(forcats)

# Sample data
adae <- data.frame(subjid = 1:5, aesev_n = c(1, 3, 2, 2, 1))

# Creating a factor
adae <- adae %>%
  mutate(
    aesev = factor(
      aesev_n,
      levels = c(1, 2, 3),
      labels = c("Mild", "Moderate", "Severe")
    )
  )

print(adae)

  subjid aesev_n    aesev
1      1       1     Mild
2      2       3   Severe
3      3       2 Moderate
4      4       2 Moderate
5      5       1     Mild


Why Factors are Powerful for Clinical Work: 1. Sorting: By default, R sorts characters alphabetically (Mild, Moderate, Severe). But ‘Mild’ shouldn’t come after ‘Severe’. Factors remember the underlying integer order you define in levels. This is critical for TFLs! 2. Missing levels: If an adverse event dataset doesn’t contain any “Severe” events, table(adae$aesev) in R will still show a count of 0 for Severe because R knows it’s a valid possible level. This ensures your tables don’t suddenly drop columns!

title: Replicating SAS Formats and Informats in R (Using Factors and Lookups)
text:
Method 2: Lookup Tables (Joins)
If you are mapping complex text, ICD-10 codes, or MedDRA dictionaries, you shouldn’t hard-code factors. Instead, you create a lookup table (a data frame) and join it. This is similar to creating a format from a dataset in SAS (cntlin).
/* SAS Code */
proc sql;
  create table adae_mapped as
  select a.*, f.term_text
  from adae a
  left join meddra_dict f
  on a.pt_code = f.pt_code;
quit;
In R, we use {dplyr}’s left_join().

# R Code
# Dictionary dataset
meddra_dict <- data.frame(
  pt_code = c(1001, 1002, 1003),
  term_text = c("Headache", "Nausea", "Fatigue")
)

# Patient data
adae <- data.frame(subjid = 1:3, pt_code = c(1002, 1001, 1002))

# Applying the format via left join
adae_mapped <- adae %>%
  left_join(meddra_dict, by = "pt_code")

print(adae_mapped)

  subjid pt_code term_text
1      1    1002    Nausea
2      2    1001  Headache
3      3    1002    Nausea


This is the standard approach for merging in decodes (e.g., merging PARAMCD and PARAM).

title: Replicating SAS Formats and Informats in R (Using Factors and Lookups)
section: Method 3: Named Vectors (The Swiss Army Knife)
text:
Method 3: Named Vectors (The Swiss Army Knife)
Sometimes you just want a quick inline format replacement without building a whole data frame. In SAS, you might use a messy if/else if/else block. In R, you can use a named vector.
A named vector is like a tiny dictionary where the “names” are your raw values, and the “values” are your formatted labels. You can use R’s subsetting [ operator to replace values quickly.

# Define our "format"
fmt_sex <- c("M" = "Male", "F" = "Female", "U" = "Unknown")

adsl <- data.frame(subjid = 1:4, sex = c("M", "F", "F", "U"))

# Apply the format by using the raw column to subset the named vector
adsl$sex_decoded <- unname(fmt_sex[adsl$sex])

print(adsl)

  subjid sex sex_decoded
1      1   M        Male
2      2   F      Female
3      3   F      Female
4      4   U     Unknown


Alternatively, in a #dplyr pipeline, you can use recode() or case_match().

adsl <- adsl %>%
  mutate(
    sex_decoded = case_match(sex, 
      "M" ~ "Male",
      "F" ~ "Female",
      "U" ~ "Unknown"
    )
  )

text:
Wrapping Up
R doesn’t give you a direct 1-to-1 substitute for PROC FORMAT. Instead, it forces you to think about what you actually want to achieve: * Need distinct ordering for tables? Use factor(). * Need to merge a dictionary of thousands of terms? Use left_join(). * Need a quick, hard-coded string replacement? Use a named vector or case_match().
You are now well-equipped to handle the primary hurdles of moving your data operations from SAS to R. Up next: Building SDTMs directly in R!

title: Safety TFLs: Creating Complex Adverse Event (AE) Summary Tables with {rtables}
text:
If you ask any clinical SAS programmer what the most tedious table to code is from scratch, 90% will say: The Adverse Event System Organ Class / Preferred Term Summary.
Let’s review the requirements for a standard Table 14.3.1.2: 1. Column headers must be Split by Treatment Arm. 2. Column headers must include (N=xx) counts down from the ADSL population. 3. Row headers must list the AEBODSYS (System Organ Class). 4. Beneath AEBODSYS, rows must indent and list the AEDECOD (Preferred Term). 5. The statistics must show n (%) where n is the number of subjects with at least one AE of that type, and % is (n / N) * 100. 6. Rows should ideally sort by frequency (highest to lowest), not alphabetically.
In SAS, this requires macro calls inside of macro calls, heavily parameterized PROC SQL joins, and intense PROC REPORT compute blocks.
Let’s do it in R using {rtables}.

title: Safety TFLs: Creating Complex Adverse Event (AE) Summary Tables with {rtables}
text:
Meet {rtables}
The {rtables} package operates on a declarative tree structure. You define the Layout first. The Layout is a set of instructions on how the table should look before data is applied.

library(dplyr)
library(rtables)

Warning: package 'rtables' was built under R version 4.4.3


Warning: package 'formatters' was built under R version 4.4.3

# Define a function to calculate incidence (n and %)
s_incidence <- function(x, .N_col) {
  # x is a vector of USUBJIDs who had the event
  # .N_col is the total number of subjects in the column (from ADSL)
  
  n <- length(unique(x)) # number of unique subjects
  pct <- if_else(.N_col == 0, 0, (n / .N_col) * 100)
  
  # Return a formatted string
  in_rows(
    "n (%)" = rcell(c(n, pct), format = "xx (xx.x%)")
  )
}

Wait, what did we just do? We created a tiny function (s_incidence) that {rtables} will call internally every time it needs to populate a cell. rcell() handles the string formatting (no PROC FORMAT or put() needed!).

title: Safety TFLs: Creating Complex Adverse Event (AE) Summary Tables with {rtables}
text:
Constructing the Layout
Now, we dictate the structure of the table.

# Define the Layout
lyt <- basic_table() %>%
  # 1. Split columns by Treatment Arm
  split_cols_by("TRTA") %>%
  
  # 2. Add the column (N=xx) counts based on the ADSL population
  add_colcounts() %>%
  
  # 3. Analyze the overall subjects with any AE at the top
  analyze_num_patients("USUBJID", .stats = "unique", .labels = c(unique = "Any Adverse Event")) %>%
  
  # 4. Split rows by System Organ Class (AEBODSYS)
  split_rows_by("AEBODSYS", split_fun = drop_split_levels) %>% # Drops empty SOCs
  summarize_row_groups() %>% # Automatically sums up the SOC level
  
  # 5. Nested within SOC, analyze the Preferred Term (AEDECOD)
  analyze("AEDECOD", afun = s_incidence) # Calls our custom function!

This layout code is remarkable. It reads exactly like the SAP mockup shell. - “Split columns by Arm” - “Add N counts” - “Analyze total patients” - “Split rows by SOC” - “Analyze Preferred Term”

title: Safety TFLs: Creating Complex Adverse Event (AE) Summary Tables with {rtables}
text:
Building and Printing the Table
Once the layout (lyt) is defined, we apply the ADAE data and the ADSL data to it.

# Mock Datasets (Pre-filtered for TEAEs only!)
adsl <- source_adsl # Must contain USUBJID and TRTA
adae <- source_adae # Must contain USUBJID, TRTA, AEBODSYS, AEDECOD

title: The Mindset Shift: Moving from SAS Data Steps to {dplyr}
text:
If you’ve spent the better part of your career looking at the familiar blueness of the SAS environment, typing out data ... set ... run;, transitioning to R can feel a bit like learning to write with your non-dominant hand. The concepts are all there, but the muscle memory is completely wrong.
The biggest hurdle for experienced SAS programmers isn’t syntax—it’s mindset.
In SAS, the Data Step processes data row-by-row (the Program Data Vector or PDV). We naturally think about “retaining” variables, “first.var” and “last.var”, and looping sequentially. In R, particularly when using the {dplyr} package (part of the {tidyverse}), we need to think in terms of vectors and pipelines.
Let’s explore this mindset shift.

The Mindset Shift: Moving from SAS Data Steps to {dplyr}
section: The R Way: Enter the Pipeline
text:
The R Way: Enter the Pipeline
In R, the {dplyr} package provides a set of “verbs” that allow you to manipulate data frames elegantly. Instead of a Data Step block, we use the pipe operator (%>% or |>) to pass data from one verb to the next.
Here is the exact same logic written in R:

library(dplyr)

# Mock ADSL Data
adsl <- data.frame(
  usubjid = c("001", "002", "003", "004"),
  arm = c("Active", "Placebo", "Active", "Placebo"),
  weight_bl = c(80, 75, 90, 85),
  weight_w12 = c(78, 76, 82, 85)
)

# R Code using dplyr
weight_change <- adsl %>%
  filter(arm == "Active") %>%
  mutate(
    pct_change = ((weight_w12 - weight_bl) / weight_bl) * 100,
    flag = if_else(pct_change >= 5, "Y", "N")
  )


Breaking It Down
Notice the shift in thinking: 1. The Pipe (%>%): Think of this as “and then.” Take adsl, and then filter it, and then mutate it. 2. filter(): This is your where statement. It operates on the whole dataset at once, returning only rows where the condition is TRUE. 3. mutate(): This creates new columns or modifies existing ones. 4. Vectorized Logic: The if_else() function applies the condition to the entire column (pct_change) simultaneously, rather than checking it row-by-row.

The transition from SAS to R is really a shift from row-wise iteration to vectorized operations on columns. Once you stop trying to force R to behave like a SAS Data Step and embrace the {dplyr} pipeline, your code will become more readable, more efficient, and surprisingly fun to write.

Keep only rows present in both tables. Equivalent to SAS Merge (A, B) with if a and b.

title: 3. Data Structures: Vectors & Frames
text:
In SAS, almost everything is a dataset. In R, you have lower-level building blocks.


The fundamental unit in R. Even a single number is a vector of length 1. Vectors must be of the same type (numeric, character, logical).
# Numeric vector
ages <- c(25, 30, 45, 22)

# Character vector
names <- c("Alice", "Bob", "Charlie")
Note: R is 1-indexed, just like SAS. ages[1] is 25.



Lists can contain anything: vectors, datasets, other lists, models. They are flexible containers.
my_patient <- list(
  id = "1001",
  visits = c("Screening", "Baseline", "Week 4"),
  demographics = data.frame(age = 45, sex = "M")
)



This is your SAS Dataset. It is technically a list of vectors of equal length.

data.frame: The base R version.
tibble: The modern (“tidyverse”) version. It prints nicer and is stricter (doesn’t change variable names or types unexpectedly).

library(tibble)

dm <- tibble(
  USUBJID = c("001", "002", "003"),
  ARM = c("Placebo", "Active", "Placebo"),
  AGE = c(45, 52, 38)
)



Factors are used for categorical data. They look like strings but are stored as integers with labels. This is similar to SAS Formats.
sex <- factor(c("M", "F", "F", "M"), levels = c("F", "M"))



In SAS, numeric missing is .. In R, it is NA. Important: NA propagates. 5 + NA equals NA. You often need na.rm = TRUE in functions.
mean(c(1, 2, NA)) # Returns NA
mean(c(1, 2, NA), na.rm = TRUE) # Returns 1.5

title: Validating SDTM Domains Programmatically in R: A New Approach
text:
Programmatic QC in R
Because R is an interactive, memory-based language, we can run validation suites directly against our data frames before we ever write them to disk. Several packages in the open-source clinical R community (like {pointblank} or {validate}) allow us to define rule sets.

Setting Up Rules with {validate}
Let’s look at how we might validate the DM domain using the {validate} package.

library(dplyr)
library(validate)

Warning: package 'validate' was built under R version 4.4.3

# Our theoretical DM domain
dm_target <- data.frame(
  STUDYID = c("ABC", "ABC", "ABC"),
  DOMAIN = c("DM", "DM", "AE"), # Intentional error here
  USUBJID = c("ABC-01", "ABC-02", "ABC-01"), # Intentional duplicate
  AGE = c(45, -5, 60), # Intentional negative age
  SEX = c("M", "F", "UNKNOWN") # Intentional non-standard codelist
)

# Define CDISC IG rules
rules <- validator(
  check_domain = DOMAIN == "DM",
  check_unique = is_unique(USUBJID),
  check_age_positive = AGE >= 0 & AGE <= 120,
  check_sex_codelist = SEX %in% c("M", "F", "U")
)

# Run the validation
qc_results <- confront(dm_target, rules)

If you write SAS code for clinical trials, you likely type PROC FREQ and PROC MEANS in your sleep. These two procedures form the backbone of exploratory data analysis, data checking, and baseline characteristic tables.
When migrating to R, SAS programmers inevitably ask: “What’s the R equivalent of PROC MEANS?”
The good news? The R ecosystem (specifically the {tidyverse}) provides tools that are just as powerful, but vastly more flexible for integration into downstream operations.
Let’s break down how to handle tabulations and summary statistics in R.

text:
If you write SAS code for clinical trials, you likely type PROC FREQ and PROC MEANS in your sleep. These two procedures form the backbone of exploratory data analysis, data checking, and baseline characteristic tables.
When migrating to R, SAS programmers inevitably ask: “What’s the R equivalent of PROC MEANS?”
The good news? The R ecosystem (specifically the {tidyverse}) provides tools that are just as powerful, but vastly more flexible for integration into downstream operations.
Let’s break down how to handle tabulations and summary statistics in R.

title: Translating PROC FREQ and PROC MEANS into R: A Practical Guide
text:
Replacing PROC FREQ
Let’s look at a standard frequency table for adverse event severity (AETOXGR).
/* SAS Code: PROC FREQ */
proc freq data=adae;
  tables aetoxgr / missing;
run;

The Base R Way
In Base R, you have the table() function, which is functional but lacks the modern structure we usually want.

# Mock ADAE Data
adae <- data.frame(
  subjid = 1:50,
  trta = sample(c("Placebo", "Active"), 50, replace = TRUE),
  aetoxgr = sample(c("MILD", "MODERATE", "SEVERE"), 50, replace = TRUE)
)

# Base R
table(adae$aetoxgr, useNA = "always")


    MILD MODERATE   SEVERE     <NA> 
      23       14       13        0 


Using {dplyr}, the replacement is the count() function. It’s elegant and returns a data frame (which SAS users appreciate, given that PROC FREQ requires an ods output statement to capture the results!).

library(dplyr)

# dplyr equivalent
adae %>%
  count(aetoxgr)

   aetoxgr  n
1     MILD 23
2 MODERATE 14
3   SEVERE 13


Need percentages like SAS provides natively? Combine count() with a simple mutate():

adae %>%
  count(aetoxgr) %>%
  mutate(percent = (n / sum(n)) * 100)

   aetoxgr  n percent
1     MILD 23      46
2 MODERATE 14      28
3   SEVERE 13      26




Cross-Tabulations
SAS:
proc freq data=adae;
  tables trta * aetoxgr;
run;
R {dplyr} + {tidyr}:

library(tidyr)

adae %>%
  count(trta, aetoxgr) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = aetoxgr, values_from = n, values_fill = 0)

# A tibble: 2 × 4
  trta     MILD MODERATE SEVERE
  <chr>   <int>    <int>  <int>
1 Active     12        7      7
2 Placebo    11        7      6


Notice how pivot_wider() reshapes the data frame exactly the way you need it for reporting—no PROC TRANSPOSE required!

title: Translating PROC FREQ and PROC MEANS into R: A Practical Guide
text:
Replacing PROC MEANS
PROC MEANS (or its twin, PROC SUMMARY) is used to calculate N, mean, standard deviation, median, min, and max.
/* SAS Code: PROC MEANS */
proc means data=advs n mean std median min max;
  class paramcd;
  var aval;
run;

The Tidyverse Way: group_by() + summarize()
In R, calculating summary statistics is a two-step pipeline: group the data, then summarize it.

# Mock ADVS Data
advs <- data.frame(
  subjid = rep(1:10, each = 2),
  paramcd = rep(c("SYSBP", "DIABP"), times = 10),
  aval = c(rnorm(10, 120, 10), rnorm(10, 80, 5))
)

# dplyr equivalent
advs %>%
  group_by(paramcd) %>%
  summarize(
    n = n(),
    mean_val = mean(aval, na.rm = TRUE),
    std_dev = sd(aval, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_val = median(aval, na.rm = TRUE),
    min_val = min(aval, na.rm = TRUE),
    max_val = max(aval, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

# A tibble: 2 × 7
  paramcd     n mean_val std_dev median_val min_val max_val
  <chr>   <int>    <dbl>   <dbl>      <dbl>   <dbl>   <dbl>
1 DIABP      10    102.     25.1      101.     72.9    139.
2 SYSBP      10     99.8    24.5       93.5    74.9    135.


Two key things to note here for SAS transplants: 1. R is unforgiving with missing data. In SAS, mean(1, 2, .) is 1.5. In R, mean(c(1, 2, NA)) is NA. You almost always need to add na.rm = TRUE to your statistical functions to skip missing values explicitly. 2. The result is inherently a tidy, structured dataset. There’s no separate “procedure output window” vs “output dataset.” You just assign the result directly: summary_stats <- advs %>% summarize(...)

title: Translating PROC FREQ and PROC MEANS into R: A Practical Guide
text:
Summarizing Multiple Variables at Once
What if you want the mean of multiple variables? SAS makes this easy by listing them in the var statement.
In R, {dplyr} provides the incredibly powerful across() function.

# R: Summarizing multiple numeric variables
advs %>%
  group_by(paramcd) %>%
  summarize(
    across(
      .cols = where(is.numeric), 
      .fns = list(
        mean = ~mean(.x, na.rm = TRUE),
        sd = ~sd(.x, na.rm = TRUE)
      ),
      .names = "{.col}_{.fn}"
    )
  )

# A tibble: 2 × 5
  paramcd subjid_mean subjid_sd aval_mean aval_sd
  <chr>         <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>   <dbl>
1 DIABP           5.5      3.03     102.     25.1
2 SYSBP           5.5      3.03      99.8    24.5


This single block of code takes every numeric column in your dataset, calculates the mean and standard deviation, and automatically names the new columns (e.g., aval_mean, aval_sd). It is essentially a programmatic macro built right into the syntax.

title: Translating PROC FREQ and PROC MEANS into R: A Practical Guide
text:
Conclusion
Letting go of PROC FREQ and PROC MEANS feels strange at first. But once you realize that R functions like count() and summarize() instantly return structured data frames instead of static printouts, you’ll wonder how you ever lived without them.
Next up: The great missing data mismatch. We’ll explore why R’s NA is a totally different beast than SAS’s period (.).

title: How to Optimize Your R Code: Best Practices in Clinical Trial Analysis
text:
A common complaint from SAS programmers transitioning to R is that R is “too slow.” They write a script to derive baseline flags on a 5-million-record lab dataset, and R grinds to a halt while SAS blazed through it.
Usually, the problem is not R. The problem is writing SAS code in R.
R is optimized for vectorized operations. If you attempt to force R to read data sequentially row-by-row (like a SAS data step), it will aggressively punish you with terrible performance.
Let’s look at the three Golden Rules of optimizing R code for clinical analysis.

title: How to Optimize Your R Code: Best Practices in Clinical Trial Analysis
How to Optimize Your R Code: Best Practices in Clinical Trial Analysis
text:
2. Memory Management: Pre-Allocation
Another classic SAS habit is creating empty data sets and iteratively appending (rbind) rows to them inside a macro loop.
In SAS, the APPEND procedure writes directly to disk. In R, everything lives in RAM.
If you rbind() a new row to a 100,000-row dataframe inside a loop, R responds by copying the entire 100,000-row dataframe in memory, adding one row, and destroying the old copy. It does this 100,000 times! This is why your memory spikes and your computer crashes.
The Solution: Use lists. R handles lists incredibly efficiently. If you must iterate, save your results to a list, and bind_rows() only once at the very end.

# 1. Pre-allocate an empty list
results_list <- list()

# 2. Assign chunks of data to list elements
for (i in 1:100) {
  # Perform some complex simulation or derivation
  temp_df <- run_complex_derivation(i)
  
  # Store the dataframe in the list (Fast!)
  results_list[[i]] <- temp_df
}

# 3. Bind them all together exactly ONE TIME
final_dataset <- bind_rows(results_list)

Alternatively, use the {purrr} package’s map_dfr() to handle this functional iteration natively.

title: How to Optimize Your R Code: Best Practices in Clinical Trial Analysis
text:
3. Avoid Re-Reading Datasets
A common inefficiency in SDTM mapping is reading the raw data multiple times. “I need to create DM, so I’ll read Demog.csv. Now I need to create VS, so I’ll read Demog.csv to get the Treatment Date.”
Because R holds objects in memory, you should adopt a modular architecture: 1. Create a 01_load_data.R script that reads all primary CSV/SAS7bDAT files into raw R datasets. 2. Build your domains (DM, VS, AE). 3. Let your scripts reference those objects naturally in the global environment.

title: How to Optimize Your R Code: Best Practices in Clinical Trial Analysis
text:
When {dplyr} Isn’t Fast Enough
For 95% of clinical trials, {dplyr} is more than fast enough. The mutate() and filter() verbs are highly optimized.
However, what if you are working with Real World Evidence (RWE) or genomic data? What if your simulated baseline dataset is 50 gigabytes with 200 million rows, and you need to calculate LOCF groupings?
In those rare, hyper-massive scenarios, {dplyr} will face bottlenecks. For those cases, we turn to the king of R performance optimization. In the next post, we will explore {data.table}.

title: Clinical Listings in R: Creating Patient Profiles that Rival PROC REPORT
text:
Building a Listing with {flextable}
The {flextable} package is designed specifically for tabular reporting in Microsoft Word and PowerPoint (and HTML/PDF). Because clinical organizations heavily rely on DOCX/RTF formats for collaborative review, this is the perfect package for listings.
Let’s build a Lab Abnormalities Listing (Table 16.2.8).

library(dplyr)
library(flextable)

Warning: package 'flextable' was built under R version 4.4.3

library(officer)

Warning: package 'officer' was built under R version 4.4.3

# Simulated Extreme Lab Values
adlb_abn <- data.frame(
  USUBJID = c("101", "101", "102", "102", "103"),
  PARAM = c("Alanine Aminotransferase", "Aspartate Aminotransferase", "Potassium", "Sodium", "Hemoglobin"),
  AVISIT = c("Week 4", "Week 4", "Baseline", "Week 12", "EOT"),
  AVAL = c(120, 85, 2.5, 150, 7.2),
  ANRIND = c("HIGH", "HIGH", "LOW", "HIGH", "LOW"),
  FLAG = c("*", "*", "*", "", "**")
)

# Create the basic flextable object
ft_listing <- flextable(adlb_abn) %>%
  
  # Format the headers
  set_header_labels(
    USUBJID = "Subject ID",
    PARAM = "Laboratory Parameter",
    AVISIT = "Visit",
    AVAL = "Result\n(Numeric)",
    ANRIND = "Reference\nIndicator",
    FLAG = "Clinical\nFlag"
  ) %>%
  
  # Styling 
  theme_vanilla() %>%
  align(align = "center", part = "all") %>%
  align(j = "PARAM", align = "left", part = "body") %>% # Left align text strings
  
  # Emphasize rows with flags
  bold(i = ~ FLAG == "**", j = "AVAL") %>%
  color(i = ~ ANRIND == "HIGH", j = "ANRIND", color = "red") %>%
  color(i = ~ ANRIND == "LOW", j = "ANRIND", color = "blue") %>%
  
  # Merge repeated Subject IDs vertically (like a BREAK variable in PROC REPORT)
  merge_v(j = "USUBJID")

# View the result (in HTML usually)
ft_listing

Subject IDLaboratory ParameterVisitResult(Numeric)ReferenceIndicatorClinicalFlag101Alanine AminotransferaseWeek 4120.0HIGH*Aspartate AminotransferaseWeek 485.0HIGH*102PotassiumBaseline2.5LOW*SodiumWeek 12150.0HIGH103HemoglobinEOT7.2LOW**


Notice the merge_v(j = "USUBJID") command. This acts exactly like the order or group option in PROC REPORT, hiding duplicate Subject IDs on subsequent rows so the reviewer’s eye tracks cleanly across the patient’s data block.

title: Clinical Listings in R: Creating Patient Profiles that Rival PROC REPORT
text:
Handling Pagination in Listings
If your listing is 500 pages long, you need column headers to repeat on every page of your RTF/Word document.
While {flextable} inherently repeats headers in MS Word when rendered, controlling exactly when a page breaks is critical for Patient Profiles (e.g., breaking the page on a new USUBJID).
To accomplish this programmatically, you use Quarto. Quarto allows you to loop through unique subjects in your R code, generate a specific {flextable} for just that subject, and insert raw Markdown page breaks (\pagebreak) into the document dynamically using knitr::asis_output().

# A conceptual example of a Quarto loop for Patient Profiles

cat("# Patient Profiles: Severe Adverse Events\n")

unique_patients <- unique(adae_severe$USUBJID)

for (pt in unique_patients) {
  
  # Subset data
  pt_data <- adae_severe %>% filter(USUBJID == pt)
  
  cat(paste("## Subject Details for", pt, "\n"))
  
  # Print flextable to Word Document
  ft <- flextable(pt_data) %>% theme_vanilla()
  print(ft)
  
  # Force a Microsoft Word Page Break!
  cat('\n\n\\pagebreak\n\n')
}

text:
The Verification Advantage
Because R treats the generation of a listing as manipulating an R object (flextable), you can run unit tests on the document generation script. Your verification programmer can programmatically assert that the output object contains exactly the right columns, values, and styling attributes before a single PDF or DOCX is ever physically opened by a user.
Tables, Figures, and Data Listings in R are completely mature. Next, we are going to look at computationally intensive optimization: How to make your R code execute at lightning speed.

The Pharmaverse solved this by releasing {teal}—a standardized framework specifically designed for exploring CDISC data intuitively.

title: How I Built an Interactive Clinical App with {teal} (And Why You Should Too)
section: Building a Basic {teal} App in 10 Minutes
text:
Building a Basic {teal} App in 10 Minutes
Let’s build an app that allows a reviewer to interactively filter Demographics and explore an Adverse Event table.

# NOTE: This code is meant to be run in a live R console/script, not evaluated statically in this blog.

library(teal)
library(teal.modules.clinical)

# 1. Provide the datasets
# We wrap them in teal_data() and tell teal to make them reproducible.
data <- teal_data()
data <- within(data, {
  ADSL <- source_adsl
  ADAE <- source_adae
})
datanames(data) <- c("ADSL", "ADAE")

# 2. Define the Application Structure
# We define an app that contains two pre-built clinical modules.
app <- init(
  data = data,
  
  # Inject the pre-built modules!
  modules = modules(
    # Module 1: An interactive Demographic Table
    tm_t_summary(
      label = "Demographic Table",
      dataname = "ADSL",
      arm_var = choices_selected(c("ARM", "SEX"), "ARM"),
      summarize_vars = choices_selected(
        c("AGE", "SEX", "RACE", "BMI"), 
        c("AGE", "SEX")
      )
    ),
    
    # Module 2: An interactive Adverse Event Table
    tm_t_events(
      label = "Adverse Event Summary",
      dataname = "ADAE",
      arm_var = choices_selected(c("ARM", "SEX"), "ARM"),
      llt = choices_selected(c("AEDECOD", "AETERM"), "AEDECOD"),
      hlt = choices_selected(c("AEBODSYS", "AESOC"), "AEBODSYS")
    )
  )
)

# 3. Launch the app!
runApp(app)

If you learn R today, you learn {dplyr}. The syntax is readable, the pipe operator (%>% or |>) flows logically from left to right, and the documentation is immaculate.

If you are dealing with a standard Phase II trial dataset (e.g., 5,000 rows in ADLB), stay with {dplyr}. You will never notice the speed difference. However, if you are doing: - Massive Real-World Evidence (RWE) database queries with 50 million rows. - High-frequency sensor data analytics (continuous glucose monitors or vital sign wearables). - Heavy Monte Carlo clinical trial simulations.
Then {data.table} is not just useful; it is mandatory.

{data.table} vs {dplyr}: When Speed Matters for Massive Clinical Datasets
text:
Syntax Comparison
The {data.table} syntax uses the fast [ operator, generally structured as DT[i, j, by]. - i: The row filter (where) - j: The column operations (select or mutate) - by: Grouping
Let’s look at three standard operations.

1. Filtering Rows (where)

library(dplyr)
library(data.table)

# dplyr
adlb_filt <- adlb %>% filter(PARAMCD == "ALT" & AVAL > 40)

# data.table
setDT(adlb) # Convert dataframe to data.table
adlb_filt_dt <- adlb[PARAMCD == "ALT" & AVAL > 40]



2. Group By and Summarize (PROC MEANS)
Let’s calculate the mean and maximum lab result by Subject and Parameter.

# dplyr
adlb_summary <- adlb %>%
  group_by(USUBJID, PARAMCD) %>%
  summarize(
    Mean_AVAL = mean(AVAL, na.rm = TRUE),
    Max_AVAL = max(AVAL, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) %>%
  ungroup()

# data.table
adlb_summary_dt <- adlb[, .(Mean_AVAL = mean(AVAL, na.rm = TRUE),
                            Max_AVAL = max(AVAL, na.rm = TRUE)), 
                        by = .(USUBJID, PARAMCD)]

Notice how {data.table} condenses the entire operation into the [i, j, by] structure. We leave i blank because we aren’t filtering. We define the summary stats in j (using .(), which is a list alias), and we group by.


3. Modifying by Reference (The := Operator)
This is the secret weapon of {data.table}. Whenever you see the walrus operator (:=), {data.table} is modifying the column directly in RAM without a deep copy.

# dplyr (Copies the dataset in memory)
adsl <- adsl %>%
  mutate(AGEGR1 = if_else(AGE > 65, ">65", "<=65"))

# data.table (Updates in place! Instantly fast, zero RAM spike)
adsl[, AGEGR1 := fifelse(AGE > 65, ">65", "<=65")]

Notice we didn’t even use adsl <-. Just executing that line updates the variable within adsl permanently.

title: {data.table} vs {dplyr}: When Speed Matters for Massive Clinical Datasets
section: Which Should You Choose for Clinical Work?
text:
Which Should You Choose for Clinical Work?
In the pharmaceutical industry, readability is paramount for verification and peer review. For this reason, {dplyr} handles 90% of clinical trial derivations (especially when using {admiral}).
However, {dplyr} provides the function dtplyr, which translates tidyverse code into {data.table} code automatically before running it! This gives you the readability of the tidyverse with the execution speed of {data.table}.
For standard Phase 1-3 trials: Stick to {dplyr}. For epidemiology, RWE, and billion-row wearable data: Master {data.table}.
Next, we shift from back-end processing to front-end magic. We will explore how to put these numbers into the hands of medical reviewers via Interactive Shiny Apps and {teal}.

title: Traceability in R: Ensuring Your ADaMs and SDTMs Meet Regulatory Standards
text:
When the FDA or EMA receives a submission, their reviewers expect a clear, unbroken chain of evidence from the final Tables, Figures, and Listings (TFLs) all the way back to the raw source data (EDC). This concept is called traceability.
Regulatory agencies don’t care if you used SAS, R, Python, or an abacus—so long as the final outputs conform strictly to CDISC standards and the lineage of the data is auditable.
Historically, SAS has dominated this space because the industry spent decades building macro libraries designed to ensure traceability. Since R is open-source and highly flexible, critics often ask: “Can R guarantee traceability?”
Yes. Here’s how.

title: Traceability in R: Ensuring Your ADaMs and SDTMs Meet Regulatory Standards

Yes. Here’s how.

title: Traceability in R: Ensuring Your ADaMs and SDTMs Meet Regulatory Standards
text:
Defining Traceability
In CDISC, traceability exists at two levels: 1. Data-level traceability: An ADaM dataset (ADAE) must contain the sequence numbers (AESEQ) that tie it back to the SDTM domain (AE). 2. Analysis-level traceability: The Define.xml document must clearly articulate the computational methods used to create derived variables.

title: Traceability in R: Ensuring Your ADaMs and SDTMs Meet Regulatory Standards
text:
Coding for Traceability in R

1. Retaining Sequence Variables
When creating an ADaM from an SDTM, you must ensure that variables like xxSEQ (Sequence Number), USUBJID, and DOMAIN are carefully preserved. In {dplyr}, this means being explicit in your select() or keep logic.

library(dplyr)
library(admiral)

# Building ADAE and ensuring traceability to AE
adae <- ae %>%
  # Merge in ADSL, but keep the core AE traceability keys
  derive_vars_merged(
    dataset_add = adsl,
    by_vars = exprs(USUBJID),
    new_vars = exprs(TRTSDT)
  ) %>%
  # Ensure AESEQ remains untouched!
  mutate(TRTEMFL = if_else(ASTDT >= TRTSDT, "Y", "N")) %>%
  select(STUDYID, USUBJID, AESEQ, AETERM, TRTSDT, ASTDT, TRTEMFL)

Never drop AESEQ in an OCCDS domain. Without it, the reviewer cannot prove which specific headache in the SDTM dataset corresponds to the TEAE flag in the ADaM dataset.


2. Traceability in Record Imputation (BDS)
In BDS domains (like ADVS), we often create new records, such as calculating an average baseline value or imputing a Last Observation Carried Forward (LOCF) visit.
When a record is mathematically invented by the programmer (it doesn’t exist in SDTM), the variable DTYPE (Derivation Type) must be populated.

adlb <- adlb %>%
  # Creating a new Baseline Average record
  derive_summary_records(
    by_vars = exprs(USUBJID, PARAMCD),
    filter = ABLFL == "Y",
    set_values_to = exprs(
      AVAL = mean(AVAL, na.rm = TRUE),
      DTYPE = "AVERAGE" # Traceability!
    )
  )

By explicitly setting DTYPE = "AVERAGE", a reviewer instantly knows this record cannot be traced back to a specific LBSEQ in the SDTM dataset, because it is an aggregate.

title: Traceability in R: Ensuring Your ADaMs and SDTMs Meet Regulatory Standards
text:
Generating Define.xml from R
The biggest traceability deliverable is the Define.xml. This metadata document acts as the map for the FDA reviewer.
In the SAS world, Pinnacle 21 Enterprise or SAS Clinical Standards Toolkit handles this.
In the R ecosystem, the pharmaverse community introduced the {metacore} and {metatools} packages. These packages ingest your data specifications (usually an Excel file) and automatically validate that your R data frames match your spec.
Furthermore, you can generate Define.xml entirely using R packages, bypassing proprietary enterprise tools if necessary.

title: Traceability in R: Ensuring Your ADaMs and SDTMs Meet Regulatory Standards
section: R Markdown and Quarto for Documentation
text:
R Markdown and Quarto for Documentation
The ultimate advantage R holds over SAS in terms of traceability is Literate Programming.
Instead of hiding data derivation decisions inside a .sas file and hoping the reviewer reads the comments, clinical programmers can use Quarto or R Markdown to mix text, code, and output seamlessly.
A reviewer doesn’t just get a dataset; they get a rendered HTML or PDF document that explicitly states: “According to SAP Section 4.1, missing partial dates were imputed to the 15th of the month. See code chunk below.”

title: Traceability in R: Ensuring Your ADaMs and SDTMs Meet Regulatory Standards
text:
Conclusion
Traceability in R is not harder than in SAS; it simply requires adopting a standardized workflow (like {admiral}) and respecting CDISC Implementation Guidelines.
With SDTM and ADaMs sorted, it’s time to move to the main event: TFL Generation!

title: BDS (Basic Data Structure) ADaMs with {admiral}: Doing What SAS Did, But Better
text:
If ADSL is the foundation and OCCDS is the occurrence log, then BDS (Basic Data Structure) is the engine room of clinical trial analysis. Datasets like ADVS (Vitals), ADLB (Labs), and ADEG (ECGs) track parameters repeatedly measured over time for each subject.
The defining characteristics of a BDS dataset are: 1. Multiple records per subject (long format). 2. A single analyzed parameter (PARAM, PARAMCD). 3. An analysis value (AVAL, AVALC). 4. Timings and visits (AVISIT, ATPT). 5. Complex baseline derivations (ABLFL, BASE).

title: BDS (Basic Data Structure) ADaMs with {admiral}: Doing What SAS Did, But Better
text:
If ADSL is the foundation and OCCDS is the occurrence log, then BDS (Basic Data Structure) is the engine room of clinical trial analysis. Datasets like ADVS (Vitals), ADLB (Labs), and ADEG (ECGs) track parameters repeatedly measured over time for each subject.
The defining characteristics of a BDS dataset are: 1. Multiple records per subject (long format). 2. A single analyzed parameter (PARAM, PARAMCD). 3. An analysis value (AVAL, AVALC). 4. Timings and visits (AVISIT, ATPT). 5. Complex baseline derivations (ABLFL, BASE).

title: BDS (Basic Data Structure) ADaMs with {admiral}: Doing What SAS Did, But Better
text:
Setting the Baseline (ABLFL)
In SAS, determining the baseline record (the last measurement taken on or before the first dose of study drug) requires a dizzying array of PROC SORT by USUBJID PARAMCD ADT ATMN, followed by if last.PARAMCD and ADT <= TRTSDT then ABLFL = 'Y'.
If there are duplicate visits or non-missing conditions, the SAS code becomes a nightmare to maintain.
With {admiral}, we use the derive_var_extreme_flag() function.

library(dplyr)
library(admiral)

Warning: package 'admiral' was built under R version 4.4.3

# Simulating Lab Data
adlb <- data.frame(
  USUBJID = c("001", "001", "001"),
  PARAMCD = c("ALT", "ALT", "ALT"),
  AVAL = c(20, 22, 45),
  ADTM = as.POSIXct(c("2024-01-01 08:00", "2024-01-10 09:00", "2024-01-20 10:00")),
  TRTSDTM = as.POSIXct(c("2024-01-10 12:00", "2024-01-10 12:00", "2024-01-10 12:00"))
)

# 1. Derive ABLFL (Analysis Baseline Flag)
# We pre-filter for baseline records, flag the last one, and join back
adlb_bl <- adlb %>% 
  filter(ADTM <= TRTSDTM) %>%
  derive_var_extreme_flag(
    by_vars = exprs(USUBJID, PARAMCD),
    order = exprs(ADTM),
    new_var = ABLFL,
    mode = "last"
  )

adlb <- adlb %>%
  left_join(adlb_bl, by = c("USUBJID", "PARAMCD", "AVAL", "ADTM", "TRTSDTM")) %>%
  mutate(ABLFL = if_else(is.na(ABLFL), "", ABLFL))

print(adlb)

  USUBJID PARAMCD AVAL                ADTM             TRTSDTM ABLFL
1     001     ALT   20 2024-01-01 08:00:00 2024-01-10 12:00:00      
2     001     ALT   22 2024-01-10 09:00:00 2024-01-10 12:00:00     Y
3     001     ALT   45 2024-01-20 10:00:00 2024-01-10 12:00:00      


Look how explicit the R code is! Group it by USUBJID and PARAMCD. Order it chronologically (ADTM). Filter for records before or exactly on the treatment start time (condition). And pick the very last one (mode = "last").

title: BDS (Basic Data Structure) ADaMs with {admiral}: Doing What SAS Did, But Better
text:
Populating BASE and CHG
Once the ABLFL flag is set to "Y" for the baseline record, we need to populate the numeric BASE value onto every record for that USUBJID and PARAMCD, so we can calculate the change from baseline (CHG).
In SAS, this requires if ABLFL = 'Y' then _BASE = AVAL; retain _BASE; BASE = _BASE.
In {admiral}:

# 2. Derive BASE (Baseline Value)
adlb <- adlb %>%
  derive_var_base(
    by_vars = exprs(USUBJID, PARAMCD),
    source_var = AVAL,
    new_var = BASE
  ) %>%
  
  # 3. Derive CHG (Change from Baseline)
  derive_var_chg()

print(adlb)

  USUBJID PARAMCD AVAL                ADTM             TRTSDTM ABLFL BASE CHG
1     001     ALT   20 2024-01-01 08:00:00 2024-01-10 12:00:00         22  -2
2     001     ALT   22 2024-01-10 09:00:00 2024-01-10 12:00:00     Y   22   0
3     001     ALT   45 2024-01-20 10:00:00 2024-01-10 12:00:00         22  23


Yes, it really is that simple. derive_var_base() automatically looks for the record where ABLFL == "Y" and propagates that AVAL to the BASE column for all records in the group. Then, derive_var_chg() is literally a pre-built wrapper that calculates AVAL - BASE.

title: BDS (Basic Data Structure) ADaMs with {admiral}: Doing What SAS Did, But Better
text:
Handling LOCF (Last Observation Carried Forward)
In oncology and other therapeutic areas, if a subject misses a visit, we often impute their value using LOCF.
In SAS, LOCF involves heavily nested data step loops and retain statements. In {admiral}, we derive new records explicitly.

# 4. Derive LOCF values for missing visits
adlb_locf <- adlb %>%
  derive_locf_records(
    dataset_expected_obs = my_expected_visits_dataset, # A dataset defining what visits should exist
    by_vars = exprs(USUBJID, PARAMCD),
    order = exprs(AVISITN)
  )

(Note: Requires a definition of standard visits, which we skip in this mock code, but the function handles the forward propagation logic seamlessly).

title: BDS (Basic Data Structure) ADaMs with {admiral}: Doing What SAS Did, But Better
text:
The Shift to Declarative Programming
When building BDS datasets in SAS, you write imperative code: you tell the computer how to do the derivation row-by-row.
When using {admiral} in R, you write declarative code: you declare what you want (e.g., derive_var_base()), and the package handles the row operations under the hood.
This results in BDS programming that is mathematically precise, faster to write, and vastly easier for a QC programmer to review.

section: The Interactive Future: Regulatory Shiny Apps
text:
The Interactive Future: Regulatory Shiny Apps
The modern solution is deploying a validated, interactive Shiny Application as part of the regulatory submission itself.
The FDA has been explicitly encouraging innovation in this space through the R Consortium’s Pilot Submissions project. We are reaching a point where sponsors can submit an open-source R package combined with a Shiny App wrapped in a Docker container.

What an Interactive Efficacy App Achieves
Imagine shifting from standard TFLs to a dynamic Efficacy Explorer Dashboard.

# A conceptual example of a custom efficacy tab in Shiny
tabPanel("Efficacy Explorer",
         sidebarLayout(
           sidebarPanel(
             selectInput("endpoint", "Select Primary Endpoint", choices = c("PFS", "OS")),
             sliderInput("age_filter", "Age Range", min = 18, max = 99, value = c(18, 99)),
             checkboxGroupInput("biomarker", "Biomarker Status", choices = c("Positive", "Negative", "Unknown"))
           ),
           mainPanel(
             plotOutput("km_plot"),      # Dynamic Survival Curve
             tableOutput("cox_model")    # Dynamic Hazard Ratio Table
           )
         )
)

In this paradigm: 1. The Reviewer controls the data: They can tweak the specific populations, endpoints, and covariates themselves. 2. Instant answers: Instead of issuing an Information Request (IR) back to the sponsor (“Please supply the Hazard Ratios for the XYZ subpopulation”) and waiting 5 days, the reviewer moves a slider in the app and gets the answer instantly.

The Demise of the Output Delivery System (ODS)
While we map the future of R, we have to look in the rearview mirror.
The SAS macro library approach to generating static .rtf outputs is inherently limited to 2D paper matrices. We try to hack interactivity using giant hyperlinked Excel documents (PROC EXPORT), but it falls flat.
Shiny Dashboards and {teal} represent a total paradigm shift from “Printing to Paper” to “Navigating Data.”

How to Prepare for the Shift
If you are a clinical data programmer looking to safeguard your career over the next ten years, simply translating your PROC REPORT knowledge to R’s {flextable} is not enough.

Master APIs & Deployment: Learn how to host Shiny applications on Posit Connect or Shiny Server. 3. Master Git & Version Control: R projects are software development environments, not just linear scripts scattered in network drive folders. 4. Learn R Packages: Understand how to wrap your repetitive clinical derivations into KnowledgeCentReggplots style internal libraries.
The shift from row-by-row procedural coding to functional data pipelines has already happened. The shift from paper outputs to interactive applications is happening right now.
Embrace the change. The tidyverse is waiting!

title: Efficacy TFLs: Survival Analysis and Kaplan-Meier Plots using {survival} and {survminer}
text:
In oncology trials, the primary efficacy endpoint is often a time-to-event variable, such as Overall Survival (OS) or Progression-Free Survival (PFS).
In SAS, analyzing these endpoints generally requires two heavy-hitting procedures: PROC LIFETEST (for generating Kaplan-Meier curves and Log-Rank tests) and PROC PHREG (for Cox Proportional Hazards modeling).
In R, the standard isn’t just “good enough”—it’s the industry standard across all academic statistics. We use the {survival} package, authored originally by Terry Therneau (who literally wrote the book on modeling survival data). We pair it with {survminer} for publication-ready graphics.

title: Efficacy TFLs: Survival Analysis and Kaplan-Meier Plots using {survival} and {survminer}
text:
In oncology trials, the primary efficacy endpoint is often a time-to-event variable, such as Overall Survival (OS) or Progression-Free Survival (PFS).
In SAS, analyzing these endpoints generally requires two heavy-hitting procedures: PROC LIFETEST (for generating Kaplan-Meier curves and Log-Rank tests) and PROC PHREG (for Cox Proportional Hazards modeling).
In R, the standard isn’t just “good enough”—it’s the industry standard across all academic statistics. We use the {survival} package, authored originally by Terry Therneau (who literally wrote the book on modeling survival data). We pair it with {survminer} for publication-ready graphics.

title: Efficacy TFLs: Survival Analysis and Kaplan-Meier Plots using {survival} and {survminer}
text:
Fitting the Model
Let’s assume our ADSL dataset contains AVAL (time in months to event) and CNSR (censor flag). Note: In {survival}, the censor indicator needs to be formulated as Event = 1 (Dead), Censor = 0 (Alive), whereas SAS sometimes defaults to the opposite.

library(dplyr)
library(survival)

Warning: package 'survival' was built under R version 4.4.3

# Simulated ADTTE (Time to Event) dataset
adtte <- data.frame(
  USUBJID = 1:200,
  TRTA = sample(c("Placebo", "Active"), 200, replace = TRUE),
  AVAL = rexp(200, rate = 0.1), # Simulated survival time
  CNSR = sample(c(0, 1), 200, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.7, 0.3)) # 0 = event, 1 = censored
)

# Convert SAS CNSR (1=Censored, 0=Event) to R Status (0=Censored, 1=Event)
adtte <- adtte %>%
  mutate(STATUS = if_else(CNSR == 0, 1, 0))

# 1. Create the Survival Object
surv_obj <- Surv(time = adtte$AVAL, event = adtte$STATUS)

# 2. Fit the Kaplan-Meier model
km_fit <- survfit(surv_obj ~ TRTA, data = adtte)

# 3. Fit a Cox Proportional Hazards Model (for Hazard Ratio)
cox_fit <- coxph(surv_obj ~ TRTA, data = adtte)

# Output summary
summary(cox_fit)

Call:
coxph(formula = surv_obj ~ TRTA, data = adtte)

  n= 200, number of events= 140

            exp(coef) exp(-coef) lower .95 upper .95
TRTAPlacebo    0.8317      1.202    0.5954     1.162

Concordance= 0.532  (se = 0.024 )

Wald test            = 1.17  on 1 df,   p=0.3

The output of summary(cox_fit) provides the Hazard Ratio (exp(coef)), the confidence intervals, and the p-values immediately. You can easily extract these using the {broom} package to populate your Table 14.2.1.X.

title: Efficacy TFLs: Survival Analysis and Kaplan-Meier Plots using {survival} and {survminer}
text:
Visualizing the Kaplan-Meier Curve
Now, for the holy grail of oncology TFLs: The Kaplan-Meier Plot.
In SAS, customizing PROC SGPLOT to include a risk table at the bottom, adjusting the censor tick marks, and formatting the p-value text is notoriously finicky.
With {survminer} in R, it is handled automatically through a clean ggplot2 wrapper.

library(survminer)

Warning: package 'ggpubr' was built under R version 4.4.3

ggsurvplot(
  fit = km_fit,
  data = adtte,
  
  # Styling the Lines
  palette = c("#0072B2", "#D55E00"), # Colorblind friendly
  size = 1.2,
  linetype = "solid",
  
  # Censor marks
  censor = TRUE,
  censor.shape = 124, # Represents a vertical tick
  censor.size = 3,
  
  # Axes & Grid
  xlim = c(0, max(adtte$AVAL)),
  break.time.by = 5,
  xlab = "Time in Months",
  ylab = "Probability of Survival",
  
  # Confidence Intervals 
  conf.int = TRUE,
  
  # Risk Table at the bottom
  risk.table = TRUE,
  risk.table.height = 0.25,
  risk.table.title = "Number at risk",
  
  # Statistical reporting
  pval = TRUE, # Automatically calculates and prints Log-rank p-value
  pval.coord = c(2, 0.2)
)









Why this is highly superior for Clinical Trials:

The Risk Table: Adding risk.table = TRUE automatically generates an aligned table beneath the plot showing subjects at risk across the time bins.
Dynamic P-Values: It inherently understands the fitted model (km_fit) and calculates the test statistic dynamically, placing it on the chart.
Themes: It inherits {ggplot2} theming, meaning your company can define a theme_company_km() and apply it globally to all charts.
